Guides

How mealtimes work

What goes on the table is up to you. Whether your child eats it, and how much, is up to them. Pressure is a poor teacher.

Key points

Share the responsibility. You choose the food, the time, and the place. Your child chooses whether to eat and how much.
A refused food usually needs more calm tries, not a replacement meal. It can take eight to fifteen pressure-free tastes to accept a new flavour, and that’s normal.
Screens, aeroplane spoons, and pudding bribes backfire. They teach children to ignore their hunger and to see sweet food as the prize.

Who decides what

Ellyn Satter’s division of responsibility is the clearest summary of responsive feeding. You offer a meal with some structure: something your child usually eats, and something they’re still getting to know. You sit down together. You don’t plead, chase them with the spoon, or cook a second lunch when the first is refused.

When a baby turns away, clamps their mouth shut, or starts playing, they’ve finished. Ending the meal then counts as a success. It’s how they learn that their own sense of fullness matters.

Try, try again

Food neophobia, a wariness of new foods, increases in the toddler years and is completely ordinary. What helps, according to the evidence, is calm, repeated exposure: the food appears, nobody makes a fuss, and it comes back next week. Praising eating and showing disappointment at refusal both add pressure.

Cooking to order, where a refusal brings out a favourite instead, teaches your child to refuse. Serve one meal. Include a ‘safe’ food so your child won’t leave hungry. Let the new food be something they’re free to ignore.

Tricks that are not worth it

Feeding while a screen distracts the baby fills the tummy but skips the learning. Bribes (‘finish this and you can have something sweet’) turn the savoury food into a chore. Hiding every vegetable so well that your child never sees one skips the learning too. A visible piece is doing its job even if it stays on the plate.

Eat together whenever you can. Children copy the people at the table far more reliably than they follow a talk about healthy food.
